lessons.title: Evaluating Models, RAG and Agents
lessons.summary: Pick the right Amazon Bedrock evaluation job type (programmatic, human, model-as-a-judge, RAG) and validate deployments before and after release.

sections.heading: Why evaluation is its own discipline
sections.body: Generative output is non-deterministic and often has no single right answer, so unit tests alone cannot tell you whether a model, prompt or retrieval change made things better. Task 5.1 of the exam guide expects you to build **evaluation systems**: repeatable jobs over a fixed dataset, scored by metrics, a judge model or humans, run before a change ships and again after it is deployed.

sections.heading: Amazon Bedrock evaluation job types
sections.body:
Amazon Bedrock evaluations offers four job types:

- **Programmatic (automatic) model evaluation** using a built-in or your own custom prompt dataset. Cheap and repeatable; good for regression checks.
- **Human-based evaluation** using your own work team or subject-matter experts. Use it when the criteria are subjective or need domain expertise (brand voice, clinical accuracy).
- **Model-as-a-judge (LLM-as-a-judge)**: a second LLM scores each response and **explains each score**. Scales like automatic evaluation but handles open-ended quality criteria.
- **RAG evaluations with LLMs** against a Bedrock knowledge base or an external RAG source. The dataset needs **ground-truth retrieved texts and responses** so both retrieval and generation can be judged.

Targets include foundation models, Bedrock Marketplace models, customized and imported models, prompt routers and Provisioned Throughput models; sources outside Bedrock can also be evaluated.

sections.heading: Choosing between them
sections.body:
| Need | Job type |
|---|---|
| Fast regression check on a known dataset | Programmatic |
| Open-ended quality at scale with reasons | Model-as-a-judge |
| Subjective or expert judgment | Human-based |
| Is the KB retrieving the right passages and is the answer grounded? | RAG evaluation |

A common pattern is to combine them: LLM-as-a-judge for breadth, a human review sample to calibrate the judge.

sections.heading: Agents and deployment validation
sections.body: Agent quality (tool selection, multi-step success) is evaluated on **sessions, traces and spans**; Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations provides this for agents. Before a prompt, model or flow change reaches all users, validate it against a **golden dataset**, then release gradually (canary or A/B) and watch metrics. Bedrock Flows and Prompt Management give you immutable **versions**, and Flows aliases let you shift and roll back traffic by repointing the alias. Synthetic workflows (for example CloudWatch Synthetics canaries) can exercise the deployed path continuously.

keyPoints: Four Bedrock evaluation job types: programmatic, human-based, model-as-a-judge, RAG evaluation with LLMs.
LLM-as-a-judge scores responses and explains each score.
RAG evaluation datasets need ground-truth retrieved texts and responses.
Use human evaluation for subjective or expert criteria.
Evaluate agents on sessions, traces and spans (AgentCore Evaluations).
Validate against a golden dataset, then canary or A/B; roll back via versions and aliases.

gotchas.trap: Use a human work team for every quality question.
gotchas.correct: Human review is slow and costly; use model-as-a-judge for scale and a human sample to calibrate it.

gotchas.trap: Judge a RAG system only by the final answer.
gotchas.correct: A RAG evaluation scores retrieval as well, which is why the dataset needs ground-truth retrieved texts.

gotchas.trap: Ship a new prompt version to all traffic once it looks good in the console.
gotchas.correct: Run it against a golden dataset, then release gradually and keep the previous version ready for rollback.

lessons.lab: Build a 30-item golden dataset for a support assistant. Run a model-as-a-judge evaluation comparing two candidate models, then a RAG evaluation against your knowledge base. Compare the judge explanations with your own ratings on 10 items to calibrate.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting GenAI Applications
lessons.summary: Diagnose throttling, guardrail blocks, grounding failures, retrieval problems, context overflow and prompt regressions using logs, traces and configuration.

sections.heading: Throttling
sections.body:
Bedrock on-demand quotas are measured in tokens per minute (TPM), tokens per day and requests per minute. At request start Bedrock deducts **input tokens + `max_tokens`** from the quota; at the end it settles actual usage, with output tokens multiplied by a model-specific **burndown rate** (billing is still for actual tokens). So a very high `max_tokens` can throttle concurrency early even when real usage is low: **lower `max_tokens`** first.

Other levers: **cross-Region inference** profiles (Geographic keeps data in a geography; Global can route to any supported commercial Region at about 10% lower cost), **service tiers** (Priority, Standard, Flex share the on-demand quota; Reserved is a TPM reservation), Provisioned Throughput, and client retries with backoff. The automatic CloudWatch dashboard "Token Counts by Model" helps confirm token pressure.

sections.heading: Guardrail blocks and grounding failures
sections.body:
When a guardrail intervenes, inspect the **guardrail trace / assessment** returned with the response and the CloudWatch Guardrails metrics to see which policy fired (content filter, denied topic, word filter, sensitive information, contextual grounding). Tune that one policy instead of disabling the guardrail.

Contextual grounding checks score **grounding** and **relevance** against a threshold (0 to 0.99); responses below it are blocked. The **Classic** tier is strict and does not support conversational use cases; the **Standard** tier does (0.7 is a suggested starting threshold) and requires guardrail cross-Region inference. Note that `UpdateGuardrail` without `tierConfig` resets the tier to Classic. Contextual grounding runs on output only, and with streaming an irrelevant response may be flagged only after it has streamed.

sections.heading: Retrieval failures
sections.body:
- **Wrong or missing passages**: revisit chunking (default about 300 tokens; fixed-size, hierarchical, semantic, none), embeddings and metadata filters; add reranking.
- **Fewer results than requested** with hierarchical chunking is expected: child chunks are replaced by their parents.
- **OpenSearch metadata filter errors**: custom filter fields must be mapped as a keyword type.
- **Aurora pgvector with selective filters**: use pgvector 0.8.0+ iterative scans.
- **S3 Vectors ingestion failures**: per-vector metadata is limited (1 KB, 35 keys), so hierarchical chunking is not recommended there.

Use a RAG evaluation to tell retrieval problems apart from generation problems.

sections.heading: Hallucination, context overflow and prompt regressions
sections.body:
Hallucination in RAG: ground the prompt in retrieved context, require citations, add a contextual grounding check, and measure with RAG evaluation. **Context window overflow** shows up as failed or truncated requests on long conversations or large retrieved context: trim or summarize history, retrieve fewer, better chunks, or choose a model with a larger context window.

For prompt problems, **model invocation logging** (disabled by default; to CloudWatch Logs and/or S3) captures prompts, responses, token counts, `identity.arn` and `requestMetadata` for calls on `bedrock-runtime`; calls on the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint are not captured. AWS X-Ray traces the request path across services. Keep prompts versioned in Prompt Management so a regression can be tied to a version and rolled back.

keyPoints: Early TPM throttling with low real usage: lower max_tokens.
Cross-Region inference spreads load; pick Geographic when data residency matters.
Read the guardrail trace/assessment to see which policy blocked.
Classic grounding is strict and not conversational; Standard supports conversations.
Hierarchical chunking can return fewer chunks than requested.
Model invocation logging is off by default and does not cover bedrock-mantle.

gotchas.trap: Throttled, so request a quota increase immediately.
gotchas.correct: Check max_tokens first: it is reserved up front and can exhaust TPM even when actual output is small.

gotchas.trap: A guardrail is blocking good answers, so remove the guardrail.
gotchas.correct: Use the trace to find the policy that fired and tune only that policy or threshold.

gotchas.trap: Invocation logs will already have the prompts we need.
gotchas.correct: Invocation logging is disabled by default; enable it before you need the data.

lessons.lab: Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs, then send requests with a deliberately high max_tokens under load and watch throttling. Lower max_tokens and compare. Add a guardrail with a contextual grounding check, trigger a block, and read the assessment in the response.

flashcards.front: What are the two kinds of cross-Region inference profile, and when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: Geographic (for example US, EU, APAC) keeps requests inside that geography, so pick it for residency rules. Global can use any supported commercial Region and is about 10% cheaper, so pick it for cost when location does not matter.

flashcards.front: What must an SCP allow for a Global cross-Region inference profile to work?
flashcards.back: The condition `"aws:RequestedRegion": "unspecified"`. For a Geographic profile the SCP must allow every destination Region in the profile.

flashcards.front: How is a cross-Region inference request priced?
flashcards.back: At the source Region price, with no extra routing charge.

flashcards.front: Where does CloudTrail log a cross-Region inference call, and how do you see where it ran?
flashcards.back: In the source Region. The field `additionalEventData.inferenceRegion` shows the Region that served it.

flashcards.front: What unit is Provisioned Throughput bought in?
flashcards.back: Model Units (MUs). Each MU gives a fixed number of input and output tokens per minute.

flashcards.front: What commitment terms does Bedrock Provisioned Throughput offer, and how is it billed?
flashcards.back: No commitment, 1 month or 6 months (longer is cheaper per hour). Billed hourly until the PT is deleted.

flashcards.front: Can you use an inference profile or batch inference with Provisioned Throughput?
flashcards.back: No. Inference profiles do not support PT, and batch inference does not run on provisioned models.

flashcards.front: Why is the Converse API useful when evaluating several models?
flashcards.back: It uses one request and response shape across Bedrock models, so switching models is mostly a change of model ID.

flashcards.front: What are the limits of Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing?
flashcards.back: It routes only between models in the same family, is optimised for English, and cannot adapt to your app-specific performance data. A configured router uses exactly two models plus a fallback.

flashcards.front: When is SageMaker AI preferred over Bedrock for hosting a model?
flashcards.back: When you need an owned endpoint (instance type, scaling), an open-weight model from JumpStart, custom adapters such as LoRA, and version control with approval and rollback in Model Registry.

flashcards.front: Which AWS tool gives a structured best-practice review of a gen AI workload?
flashcards.back: The AWS Well-Architected Tool with the Generative AI Lens.

flashcards.front: Managed Knowledge Base vs customer-managed Knowledge Base?
flashcards.back: Managed: Bedrock runs ingestion, indexing, storage and retrieval, with connectors, document-level ACLs, Smart Parsing and Agentic Retrieval (recommended). Customer-managed: you bring and operate the vector store.

flashcards.front: Which Managed KB connector does not support document-level ACL filtering?
flashcards.back: Web Crawler. S3, SharePoint, Confluence, Google Drive and OneDrive do.

flashcards.front: Which vector stores support binary embeddings for Bedrock KBs?
flashcards.back: Only OpenSearch Serverless and OpenSearch Service managed clusters.

flashcards.front: What are the OpenSearch requirements for a Bedrock Knowledge Base?
flashcards.back: The faiss engine (nmslib is not supported); managed domains must use public access (VPC-only is not supported); custom filter fields need keyword mapping.

flashcards.front: When is Amazon S3 Vectors a good vector store, and what are its limits?
flashcards.back: Low cost with sub-second queries, best for infrequent queries. Float embeddings only (cosine or Euclidean); metadata limited to 1 KB and 35 keys per vector, so hierarchical chunking is not recommended.

flashcards.front: Which indexes does Aurora PostgreSQL need as a KB vector store?
flashcards.back: An HNSW index on the embedding column, a GIN index on the text column (for hybrid search) and a GIN index on custom_metadata. The cluster must be in the same account, with credentials in Secrets Manager.

flashcards.front: An Aurora-backed KB returns too few results when a selective metadata filter is used. Fix?
flashcards.back: Use pgvector 0.8.0 or later with iterative scans.

flashcards.front: What vector dimensions does Titan Text Embeddings V2 support?
flashcards.back: 1,024, 512 or 256. (Titan Embeddings G1 is 1,536; Cohere Embed is 1,024.)

flashcards.front: What is the default chunking strategy for a Bedrock KB?
flashcards.back: About 300 tokens per chunk, keeping sentence boundaries.

flashcards.front: Why can hierarchical chunking return fewer results than numberOfResults?
flashcards.back: Child chunks are matched and then replaced by their parent chunks; several children can share one parent.

flashcards.front: What is the trade-off of semantic chunking?
flashcards.back: Better splits on meaning, but it costs extra because it uses a foundation model during ingestion.

flashcards.front: What do you lose with the "no chunking" strategy?
flashcards.back: Each document becomes one chunk, and citations have no page numbers.

flashcards.front: How do you apply custom chunking or enrichment logic in a Bedrock KB?
flashcards.back: Add a custom transformation Lambda function to the ingestion step.

flashcards.front: How do you restrict KB retrieval to one tenant's documents?
flashcards.back: Store a tenant attribute as document metadata and pass a metadata filter on Retrieve or RetrieveAndGenerate (or use document-level ACLs in a Managed KB).

flashcards.front: An OpenSearch-backed KB fails a metadata filter with a "Rewrite first" error. Why?
flashcards.back: The custom metadata field is not mapped as a keyword type.

flashcards.front: When do you add a reranking model to retrieval?
flashcards.back: When relevant chunks are retrieved but ranked too low; the reranker rescores candidates against the query.

flashcards.front: Which KB option suits questions that depend on relationships between entities?
flashcards.back: GraphRAG with an Amazon Neptune Analytics graph. For multi-hop questions in a Managed KB, Agentic Retrieval is the other option.

flashcards.front: Which services discover and redact PII in a gen AI data pipeline?
flashcards.back: Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data in S3; Amazon Comprehend detects and redacts PII in text. Guardrails sensitive information filters protect prompts and responses at runtime.

flashcards.front: Which service validates data quality before it is ingested?
flashcards.back: AWS Glue Data Quality (rules for completeness, format, freshness).

flashcards.front: Is Bedrock model invocation logging on by default, and where can it write?
flashcards.back: Off by default. It writes to CloudWatch Logs and/or S3 in the same account and Region; bodies over 100 KB and binary data go to S3 only.

flashcards.front: Which Bedrock endpoint's calls are not captured by model invocation logging?
flashcards.back: The bedrock-mantle endpoint. Calls on bedrock-runtime (Converse, InvokeModel, streaming and OpenAI-compatible APIs) are captured.

flashcards.front: How do Bedrock Flows handle rollback?
flashcards.back: Apps call InvokeFlow on an alias that points to an immutable version; roll back by repointing the alias to the previous version.

flashcards.front: What does Bedrock Prompt Management provide?
flashcards.back: Prompts with variables, side-by-side variants, immutable versions, prompt optimization, a prompt caching option, and reuse in inference or Flow prompt nodes.

flashcards.front: What is Amazon Bedrock AgentCore?
flashcards.back: A set of modular services for building, running and operating agents, usable with any framework and any model, inside or outside Amazon Bedrock.

flashcards.front: Status of Amazon Bedrock Agents (Agents Classic)
flashcards.back: Maintenance mode: closed to new customers from July 30, 2026, frozen model catalog, no new features. Existing agents keep working with no end-of-life date.

flashcards.front: For a new agent build, what should you choose instead of a new Bedrock Agent?
flashcards.back: AgentCore: Harness for a config-based agent, or your own agent code on AgentCore Runtime.

flashcards.front: AgentCore Runtime
flashcards.back: Serverless hosting for agent code with session isolation, fast cold starts, long-running async agents, and MCP and A2A protocol support.

flashcards.front: AgentCore Harness
flashcards.back: A managed agent loop from one API call: you declare the model, system prompt and tools inline. Each session runs in its own microVM.

flashcards.front: AgentCore Memory
flashcards.back: Short-term memory for multi-turn context within a session, and long-term memory across sessions, with configurable strategies.

flashcards.front: AgentCore Gateway
flashcards.back: Turns APIs, Lambda functions and OpenAPI specs into MCP tools, and connects existing MCP servers.

flashcards.front: AgentCore Policy
flashcards.back: Deterministic rules enforced at the Gateway on every tool call, written in natural language or a Cedar-compatible language.

flashcards.front: AgentCore Identity
flashcards.back: Agent identity and authentication so agents can act with delegated user access; works with IdPs such as Cognito, Okta, Entra ID and Auth0.

flashcards.front: AgentCore Code Interpreter vs Browser
flashcards.back: Code Interpreter: sandbox for running Python, JavaScript and TypeScript. Browser: managed cloud browser (Playwright, BrowserUse) for web interaction.

flashcards.front: AgentCore Observability vs Evaluations
flashcards.back: Observability: OpenTelemetry-compatible traces in CloudWatch. Evaluations: scores agent and tool quality over sessions, traces and spans.

flashcards.front: Classic action groups map to what in AgentCore?
flashcards.back: Gateway MCP tools.

flashcards.front: Classic return of control / AMAZON.UserInput maps to what in AgentCore?
flashcards.back: Inline function tools.

flashcards.front: Where should you host your own MCP servers (per the exam guide)?
flashcards.back: AWS Lambda for lightweight, stateless MCP servers; Amazon ECS for more complex ones.

flashcards.front: In tool use, who executes the tool?
flashcards.back: Your application or the agent runtime. The model only proposes the tool name and arguments, which should be treated as untrusted input.

flashcards.front: Bedrock Flows lifecycle
flashcards.back: Working draft, prepare, test, publish an immutable version, then point an alias at it. Apps call InvokeFlow on the alias.

flashcards.front: How do you roll back a Bedrock Flow?
flashcards.back: Repoint its alias to the previous version. No application change is needed.

flashcards.front: Bedrock Flows vs Prompt Flows
flashcards.back: Same service. The exam guide uses the old name, Prompt Flows; current docs say Amazon Bedrock Flows.

flashcards.front: Step Functions pattern for human approval
flashcards.back: A task that waits for a callback with a task token, then resumes when the approver responds.

flashcards.front: Step Functions Standard vs Express
flashcards.back: Standard: long-running (up to a year), auditable processes. Express: high-volume, short-lived work (up to five minutes).

flashcards.front: How do you avoid throttling when event bursts trigger model calls?
flashcards.back: Buffer requests in Amazon SQS and limit consumer concurrency; retry throttles with exponential backoff and jitter.

flashcards.front: Batch inference basics
flashcards.back: Asynchronous: input files in S3, output to S3, completion events through EventBridge. Not supported on provisioned models.

flashcards.front: Batch inference job needs tool calling: which invocation type?
flashcards.back: InvokeModel. Tool calling is not supported with the Converse invocation type in batch.

flashcards.front: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management features
flashcards.back: Prompt variables, variants compared side by side, immutable versions, prompt optimization, and a prompt caching option; usable in inference or a Flow prompt node.

flashcards.front: Converse vs InvokeModel
flashcards.back: Converse: one message, tool and parameter format across models. InvokeModel: the provider's native request body for model-specific features.

flashcards.front: What does streaming (ConverseStream) improve?
flashcards.back: Time to first token the user sees. It does not shorten total generation time.

flashcards.front: Which endpoint's calls are NOT captured by model invocation logging?
flashcards.back: The bedrock-mantle endpoint. Use bedrock-runtime when you need invocation logs.

flashcards.front: Why can a very high max_tokens cause throttling?
flashcards.back: Input tokens plus max_tokens are reserved against the TPM quota when a request starts, which reduces how many requests fit at once.

flashcards.front: Intelligent Prompt Routing limits
flashcards.back: Routes between models in the same family only, is optimized for English, and does not adapt to your application's own performance data.

flashcards.front: GenAI gateway pattern
flashcards.back: A central entry point (API Gateway or AppSync with Cognito auth) in front of Bedrock that applies quotas, model choice, guardrails, logging and cost attribution.

flashcards.front: Name the six Amazon Bedrock Guardrails safeguards.
flashcards.back: Content filters (incl. Prompt Attack), denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters, contextual grounding checks, Automated Reasoning checks.

flashcards.front: Which content filter category targets jailbreak and injection attempts?
flashcards.back: Prompt Attack.

flashcards.front: Denied topic vs word filter: when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Denied topic for a subject described semantically (definition + sample phrases); word filter for exact words or the managed profanity list.

flashcards.front: What two actions can a sensitive information filter take on PII?
flashcards.back: Block the content or mask (anonymize) the entity. Custom regex patterns cover organization-specific identifiers.

flashcards.front: How do you apply a Bedrock guardrail to a model hosted outside Bedrock?
flashcards.back: Call the ApplyGuardrail API on the input and output text; it evaluates content without invoking a model.

flashcards.front: What does input tagging (guardContent) do?
flashcards.back: Limits guardrail evaluation to the tagged part of the prompt (for example the user turn). It is SDK only.

flashcards.front: Contextual grounding: what do the two scores measure?
flashcards.back: Grounding: is the response supported by the source? Relevance: does the response answer the query?

flashcards.front: What three inputs does a contextual grounding check need, and where does it run?
flashcards.back: Grounding source, query, and content to guard. It runs on model output only.

flashcards.front: Contextual grounding actions?
flashcards.back: BLOCK, or NONE (detect only), which is useful when calibrating thresholds.

flashcards.front: What does the Standard safeguard tier require that Classic does not?
flashcards.back: Guardrail cross-Region inference (a guardrail profile).

flashcards.front: Name three features only the Standard tier offers.
flashcards.back: Broad language support, longer denied-topic definitions, prompt leakage detection, harmful-content detection in code elements, conversational grounding.

flashcards.front: What happens if UpdateGuardrail is called without tierConfig?
flashcards.back: The tier resets to CLASSIC.

flashcards.front: Does a guardrail evaluate reasoning content blocks?
flashcards.back: No. Don't show raw reasoning to users unless you check it separately.

flashcards.front: How do you enforce a guardrail across every account in an AWS organization?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policy (BEDROCK_POLICY) that references a numeric guardrail version; the guardrail needs a resource-based policy granting bedrock:ApplyGuardrail.

flashcards.front: How do org, account and request guardrails combine?
flashcards.back: As a union; the most restrictive control wins.

flashcards.front: Which guardrail safeguard is not supported in enforced guardrails?
flashcards.back: Automated Reasoning checks.

flashcards.front: What is indirect prompt injection?
flashcards.back: Malicious instructions hidden in content the model reads (retrieved documents, web pages, emails, tool results) rather than typed by the user.

flashcards.front: What VPC endpoint type do you use for private access to Amazon Bedrock?
flashcards.back: An interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink). Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.

flashcards.front: Two controls that restrict Bedrock calls to an approved network path and approved models?
flashcards.back: A VPC endpoint policy that allows only approved model ARNs, and IAM policies with an aws:SourceVpce condition.

flashcards.front: CloudTrail vs model invocation logging?
flashcards.back: CloudTrail: who called which API, when and from where. Invocation logging: prompt and response bodies, token counts, identity.arn, requestMetadata.

flashcards.front: Default state and destinations of Bedrock model invocation logging?
flashcards.back: Disabled by default. CloudWatch Logs and/or S3, in the same account and Region.

flashcards.front: Where do invocation log bodies over 100 KB or binary data go?
flashcards.back: S3 only.

flashcards.front: Which endpoint's calls are NOT captured by model invocation logging?
flashcards.back: bedrock-mantle.

flashcards.front: Macie vs Comprehend for PII?
flashcards.back: Macie discovers sensitive data stored in S3; Comprehend detects and redacts PII in text, for example in a preprocessing pipeline.

flashcards.front: What does a SageMaker AI model card record?
flashcards.back: Intended use, risk rating, training details and evaluation results: governance documentation for review and approval.

flashcards.front: What are the two types of prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock?
flashcards.back: **Implicit** (automatic, best effort) and **explicit** (you set cache checkpoints: `cachePoint` in Converse, `cache_control` in InvokeModel).

flashcards.front: Where should a prompt cache checkpoint go?
flashcards.back: After the stable prefix (tools, system prompt, reference content). The prefix must reach the model's minimum token count, counted cumulatively tools then system then messages.

flashcards.front: Can prompt caching be used with batch inference?
flashcards.back: No. Prompt caching applies to on-demand inference only.

flashcards.front: Which response fields confirm prompt cache behaviour?
flashcards.back: `cacheWriteInputTokens` (written to cache) and `cacheReadInputTokens` (served from cache).

flashcards.front: Bedrock batch inference: inputs, outputs and notifications?
flashcards.back: Asynchronous job reading input files from S3 and writing results to S3. Use EventBridge for job state-change events. Not supported for provisioned models.

flashcards.front: How is Provisioned Throughput purchased and billed?
flashcards.back: In **model units** (each gives set input/output tokens per minute), billed hourly, with no-commitment, 1-month or 6-month terms. Billing runs until you delete it.

flashcards.front: Name the four inference service tiers and when to use each.
flashcards.back: **Reserved** (committed TPM, 1 or 3 months), **Priority** (fastest, premium), **Standard** (default), **Flex** (discounted, latency-tolerant work like evals).

flashcards.front: What does model distillation do?
flashcards.back: A larger teacher model generates responses used to fine-tune a smaller, cheaper student model. Invocation logs can be the input. The result is private to your account.

flashcards.front: What are the limits of Intelligent Prompt Routing?
flashcards.back: Routes only between models in the same family, optimized for English, and cannot adapt to app-specific performance data. Configured routers use two models plus a fallback.

flashcards.front: Global vs Geographic cross-Region inference?
flashcards.back: Global routes to any supported commercial Region (about 10% cheaper). Geographic keeps data inside a geography (US, EU, APAC); choose it for residency rules.

flashcards.front: Is Bedrock model invocation logging on by default?
flashcards.back: No. It is disabled by default. Destinations are CloudWatch Logs and/or S3 in the same account and Region.

flashcards.front: Where do invocation log bodies over 100 KB go?
flashcards.back: S3 only (also binary data). CloudWatch Logs receives the smaller text entries.

flashcards.front: How do you attribute Bedrock token usage to tenants or features?
flashcards.back: Pass `requestMetadata` on calls; invocation logs record it with `identity.arn` and token counts, so Logs Insights can aggregate by tag or principal.

flashcards.front: What does Bedrock deduct from the token quota at the start of a request?
flashcards.back: Input tokens plus `max_tokens`. At the end it settles to input + cache write + output x burndown rate. Cache reads do not count.

flashcards.front: First fix for TPM throttling at low actual output?
flashcards.back: Lower `max_tokens` to realistic values; the start-of-request reservation is exhausting the quota.

flashcards.front: Which CloudWatch dimensions show the service tier that served a request?
flashcards.back: `ServiceTier` (requested) and `ResolvedServiceTier` (actually served).

flashcards.front: What are the four Amazon Bedrock evaluation job types?
flashcards.back: Programmatic (automatic) model evaluation, human-based evaluation, model-as-a-judge (LLM-as-a-judge), and RAG evaluations with LLMs.

flashcards.front: What does a model-as-a-judge evaluation produce for each response?
flashcards.back: A score from a second LLM plus an explanation of that score.

flashcards.front: What must a RAG evaluation dataset contain?
flashcards.back: Prompts with ground-truth retrieved texts and ground-truth responses, so both retrieval and generation can be judged.

flashcards.front: When should you choose human-based evaluation?
flashcards.back: When criteria are subjective or need domain expertise; use your own work team or SMEs. Often used to calibrate an LLM judge.

flashcards.front: Where are agents evaluated in AgentCore, and on what?
flashcards.back: AgentCore Evaluations scores agent and tool quality on sessions, traces and spans.

flashcards.front: Why can a high max_tokens cause throttling when actual usage is low?
flashcards.back: Bedrock deducts input tokens + max_tokens from the TPM quota at request start, so oversized max_tokens reserves quota that is never used.

flashcards.front: Which cross-Region inference profile fits a data-residency requirement?
flashcards.back: A Geographic profile (for example EU), which keeps processing within that geography. Global routes to any supported commercial Region.

flashcards.front: How do you find which guardrail policy blocked a response?
flashcards.back: Inspect the guardrail trace/assessment returned with the response and the CloudWatch Guardrails metrics.

flashcards.front: Contextual grounding: Classic vs Standard tier for chatbots?
flashcards.back: Classic is strict and does not support conversational use cases; Standard does (suggested start threshold 0.7) and requires guardrail cross-Region inference.

flashcards.front: Why can hierarchical chunking return fewer results than requested?
flashcards.back: Retrieved child chunks are replaced by their parent chunks, so several children can collapse into one parent.

flashcards.front: Is Bedrock model invocation logging on by default?
flashcards.back: No. You must enable it (CloudWatch Logs and/or S3). It covers bedrock-runtime APIs, not the bedrock-mantle endpoint.

flashcards.front: How do you safely roll out a new Bedrock Flow version?
flashcards.back: Publish an immutable version, validate it on a golden dataset, shift traffic gradually, and roll back by repointing the alias to the previous version.

questions.scenario: EU claims assistant
questions.stem: An insurer runs a claims assistant on Amazon Bedrock in an EU Region. Policy says customer data must not be processed outside the EU. At peak hours the app hits on-demand throttling in its home Region. What should the developer do?
options: Move the workload to batch inference so throttling no longer applies
Call a Global cross-Region inference profile to get the most capacity and a lower price
Retry throttled requests against the same model in a US Region
Call an EU Geographic cross-Region inference profile instead of the model ID
questions.explanation: A Geographic profile spreads requests across Regions inside one geography, which adds capacity while keeping data in the EU. A Global profile can route to any commercial Region, which breaks the residency rule.
rationales: Batch inference is asynchronous and does not fit an interactive claims assistant.
Global profiles may run requests in any supported commercial Region, violating the EU-only policy.
Manually failing over to a US Region sends customer data outside the EU.
Correct: more capacity, and requests stay within the EU geography.

questions.scenario: Org-wide Region SCP
questions.stem: A company's SCP denies every request whose aws:RequestedRegion is not in an approved list. Developers switch from a model ID to a Global cross-Region inference profile, and calls start failing with access denied, while direct model calls in the home Region still work. What is the fix?
options: Enable every commercial Region in the account manually
Attach bedrock:InvokeModel permission to the developers' IAM role
Buy Provisioned Throughput and attach it to the Global profile
Add the condition value "unspecified" for aws:RequestedRegion to the SCP's allowed values
questions.explanation: Global cross-Region inference requires the SCP to allow aws:RequestedRegion = "unspecified". Requests can route to Regions that are not manually enabled, so enabling Regions is not the issue.
rationales: CRIS can route to Regions that are not manually enabled; the SCP denial is the blocker.
Direct calls already work, so the IAM permission exists; the SCP is denying the request.
Inference profiles do not support Provisioned Throughput.
Correct: this is the documented SCP requirement for Global profiles.

questions.scenario: Audit of inference location
questions.stem: A compliance auditor asks for proof of which AWS Region actually processed specific requests sent through a Geographic cross-Region inference profile. Where should the developer look?
options: CloudTrail events in each destination Region of the profile
CloudTrail events in the source Region, using the additionalEventData.inferenceRegion field
VPC Flow Logs for the application subnets
The Bedrock console's Provisioned Throughput page
questions.explanation: CloudTrail records cross-Region inference calls in the source Region, and additionalEventData.inferenceRegion shows where the request ran. Destination Regions are not where the event is logged.
rationales: Events are logged in the source Region, not in each destination Region.
Correct: source-Region CloudTrail plus the inferenceRegion field answers the question.
Flow logs show network traffic from your VPC, not the Region Bedrock used.
Provisioned Throughput is unrelated to cross-Region routing.

questions.scenario: Steady document classifier
questions.stem: A bank classifies a steady, predictable stream of documents around the clock with one Bedrock model in one Region. Throttling is unacceptable, and the team expects the workload to run for at least a year. Which option best fits?
options: Nightly batch inference jobs
A Global cross-Region inference profile with client retries
Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment, renewed as needed
Provisioned Throughput with no commitment, created only during business hours
questions.explanation: Steady, predictable, throttle-sensitive traffic is the case for dedicated Provisioned Throughput, and longer terms cost less per hour. Round-the-clock traffic rules out turning capacity on only for business hours.
rationales: The stream is continuous, not a nightly offline job.
CRIS adds burst capacity but gives no dedicated throughput guarantee.
Correct: dedicated capacity at the lower long-term hourly rate.
The workload runs around the clock, and no-commitment pricing is the highest hourly rate.

questions.scenario: Forgotten test capacity
questions.stem: A team created no-commitment Provisioned Throughput for a two-day load test. A month later the finance team sees hourly charges for it even though no traffic was sent after the test. Why?
options: The cross-Region inference profile kept routing traffic to the PT
Provisioned Throughput is billed hourly until it is deleted, regardless of traffic
No-commitment PT automatically converted to a 1-month term after 48 hours
Model invocation logging was left enabled and is billed per hour
questions.explanation: PT billing runs hourly until the PT is deleted. Unused capacity still costs money, so test PT should be deleted when the test ends.
rationales: Inference profiles do not support PT, and no traffic was sent.
Correct: billing stops only when the PT is deleted.
The documented behaviour is continued billing, not term conversion.
Invocation logging costs come from log storage, not hourly PT charges.

questions.scenario: Capacity planning review
questions.stem: An architect is reviewing a design that uses Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput. Which statements are accurate? (Select two.)
options: Batch inference jobs can run on Provisioned Throughput to use idle capacity overnight
A cross-Region inference profile can target a Provisioned Throughput model to add failover
Commitment terms are no commitment, 1 month or 6 months, with longer terms costing less per hour
Provisioned Throughput is purchased in Model Units that each provide a set token throughput per minute
questions.explanation: PT is bought in Model Units with fixed input and output tokens per minute, on no-commitment, 1-month or 6-month terms. Inference profiles do not support PT, and batch inference does not run on provisioned models.
rationales: Batch inference is not supported for provisioned models.
Inference profiles do not support Provisioned Throughput.
Correct: these are the documented terms, and longer is cheaper per hour.
Correct: Model Units define PT capacity.

questions.scenario: Archive summaries
questions.stem: A media company needs summaries for about a million archived articles. Results are needed within a few days, and cost matters more than latency. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Use the ConverseStream API so responses arrive faster
Buy Provisioned Throughput and run batch inference jobs on it
Call InvokeModel in a tight loop from a large EC2 fleet using on-demand capacity
Submit Bedrock batch inference jobs with input and output in S3 and an EventBridge rule for job status
questions.explanation: Batch inference is the asynchronous option for large offline jobs: inputs and outputs live in S3 and EventBridge reports job state changes. Batch does not run on provisioned models.
rationales: Streaming improves perceived latency for interactive use, not bulk throughput or cost.
Batch inference is not supported on provisioned models.
A tight on-demand loop will hit quotas and adds orchestration work for no benefit.
Correct: asynchronous, S3-based, suited to latency-tolerant bulk work.

questions.scenario: Batch job with tools
questions.stem: A batch inference job built with the Converse invocation type fails because each record defines tools the model should call. The team wants to keep using batch inference. What should they change?
options: Rebuild the input records using the InvokeModel invocation type with the tool definitions in the model-specific body
Remove the S3 output location so results stream back to the caller
Switch the job to Provisioned Throughput
Split the job into smaller files of the same Converse format
questions.explanation: Tool calling is not supported for batch jobs that use the Converse invocation type; the InvokeModel type must be used instead. Provisioned models cannot run batch jobs at all.
rationales: Correct: InvokeModel-format records support tool calling in batch.
Batch output always goes to S3; it does not stream back.
Batch inference is not supported for provisioned models.
File size is not the problem; the Converse invocation type is.

questions.scenario: Model bake-off
questions.stem: A team must choose between three Bedrock models from different providers for a support summarisation feature. They want to compare quality, latency and cost with the least code change and a repeatable score. What should they do?
options: Deploy each model to its own SageMaker AI endpoint and compare instance metrics
Call the models through the Converse API, changing only the model ID, and score outputs with a Bedrock evaluation job on a shared prompt dataset
Pick the largest model, since it will have the best quality
Fine-tune each model on company data first so the comparison is fair
questions.explanation: The Converse API keeps one request shape across models, and an evaluation job on a common dataset gives repeatable scores. Fine-tuning or self-hosting adds work before the basic choice is even made.
rationales: These are Bedrock models; self-hosting them adds operations and does not measure answer quality.
Correct: minimal code change plus repeatable evaluation.
Largest is not automatically best for quality per cost or latency.
Customisation is a later step and is costly before a baseline exists.

questions.scenario: Cost-aware routing
questions.stem: An English-language customer support app uses a large model from one model family. Most questions are simple. The team wants a single endpoint that sends easy prompts to a smaller model in the same family without writing routing code. Which option fits, and what is a documented limitation?
options: A Global cross-Region inference profile; it only works for English prompts
Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing; it cannot adapt routing to the app's own performance data
Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing; it can only route between models from different providers
Provisioned Throughput with two Model Units; one MU must be idle as a fallback
questions.explanation: Intelligent Prompt Routing routes between models in the same family based on predicted response quality, and is optimised for English. It cannot learn from app-specific performance data.
rationales: Cross-Region inference spreads load across Regions; it does not choose between models.
Correct: right feature, and the stated limitation is documented.
Routing is within one model family, not across providers.
Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity; it does not route by difficulty.

questions.scenario: Owned model lifecycle
questions.stem: A healthcare company must host an open-weight model with its own LoRA adapters, control the instance type, and keep an auditable record of which adapter version was approved for production so it can roll back quickly. Which approach meets these needs?
options: Use Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing between the base model and the adapter
Call the base model on Bedrock on-demand and store adapter files in an S3 bucket with versioning
Deploy from SageMaker JumpStart to a SageMaker AI endpoint and track adapter versions with approval status in SageMaker Model Registry
Use Bedrock Prompt Management versions to track adapter changes
questions.explanation: SageMaker AI gives control over the endpoint and supports adapter-based customisation, and Model Registry records versions with approval status for promotion and rollback. Prompt versions and S3 object versions do not model approval of a deployed model.
rationales: Prompt routing selects between models in a family; it does not host adapters.
On-demand Bedrock does not give instance control, and S3 versioning is not an approval workflow.
Correct: owned endpoint plus governed model versioning.
Prompt Management versions prompts, not model weights.

questions.scenario: Design review
questions.stem: Before a production launch, an architect wants a structured, AWS-defined review of a gen AI application's design against best practices. What should they use?
options: SageMaker Clarify bias reports
Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs
The AWS Well-Architected Tool with the Generative AI Lens
AWS Trusted Advisor cost checks
questions.explanation: The Generative AI Lens in the Well-Architected Tool is AWS's design-review framework for gen AI workloads. Evaluation jobs and Clarify measure model behaviour, not architecture.
rationales: Clarify analyses bias and explainability, not architecture.
Evaluation jobs score model outputs, not the overall architecture.
Correct: this is the official design-review mechanism named in the exam guide.
Trusted Advisor checks account resources, not gen AI design practices.

questions.scenario: Intranet assistant
questions.stem: An enterprise wants a RAG assistant over SharePoint and Confluence content. Employees must only get answers from documents they can already open in those systems, and the team wants minimal infrastructure to run. Which design fits best?
options: A customer-managed Knowledge Base on Aurora PostgreSQL with a prompt instruction to respect permissions
Copy all pages into one S3 bucket and use a single Knowledge Base for everyone
A Managed Knowledge Base using the SharePoint and Confluence connectors with document-level ACL filtering
A Managed Knowledge Base using the Web Crawler connector against the intranet URLs
questions.explanation: Managed Knowledge Bases provide connectors for SharePoint and Confluence and apply document-level ACL filtering, with Bedrock running the infrastructure. Web Crawler is the connector that does not support ACL filtering.
rationales: A prompt instruction is not an access control, and you operate the store yourself.
Flattening into S3 loses the per-user permissions.
Correct: managed operations plus source-system permissions.
Web Crawler sources do not support document-level ACL filtering.

questions.scenario: Archive search
questions.stem: A legal team needs semantic search over a very large archive that is queried only a few times a week. Sub-second responses are fine and storage cost is the main concern. Which vector store should back the customer-managed Knowledge Base?
options: Amazon S3 Vectors
Amazon Neptune Analytics
Amazon OpenSearch Serverless with binary embeddings
Redis Enterprise Cloud
questions.explanation: S3 Vectors is documented as a low-cost store with sub-second queries that suits infrequent querying. Neptune Analytics is for graph-based retrieval rather than plain semantic search.
rationales: Correct: low cost and suited to infrequent queries.
Neptune Analytics is for GraphRAG over relationships, not a plain low-cost archive.
A valid store, but the scenario points to the lowest-cost option for infrequent queries.
A valid store, but not the documented fit for a cheap, rarely queried archive.

questions.scenario: Shrinking the index
questions.stem: A team wants to use binary embeddings to cut vector storage for a Knowledge Base that currently uses Amazon S3 Vectors. What must they do?
options: Enable binary embeddings in the S3 Vectors index settings
Use hierarchical chunking so fewer vectors are stored
Move the vector store to OpenSearch Serverless or an OpenSearch managed cluster
Switch the distance metric in S3 Vectors from cosine to Euclidean
questions.explanation: Binary embeddings are supported only on OpenSearch Serverless and OpenSearch managed clusters. S3 Vectors accepts float embeddings only.
rationales: S3 Vectors supports float embeddings only.
Hierarchical chunking is not recommended with S3 Vectors and does not change embedding type.
Correct: only OpenSearch stores support binary embeddings.
The distance metric does not change the embedding data type.

questions.scenario: Failed ingestion
questions.stem: A Knowledge Base backed by Amazon S3 Vectors uses hierarchical chunking. Ingestion fails for documents that carry many custom metadata attributes. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: S3 Vectors does not support metadata; move all attributes into the document text
The embeddings model dimension is too small; switch to 1,536 dimensions
The per-vector metadata limit (1 KB, 35 keys) is exceeded; reduce metadata and use default or fixed-size chunking
Hierarchical chunking requires the semantic chunking FM to be enabled
questions.explanation: S3 Vectors limits metadata per vector to 1 KB and 35 keys, and hierarchical chunking is not recommended because it adds metadata. Trimming metadata and using a non-hierarchical strategy addresses the failure.
rationales: S3 Vectors supports metadata, within limits.
Dimension is unrelated to metadata size failures.
Correct: matches the documented S3 Vectors limits and guidance.

Drop the GIN index on custom_metadata

Keep 1,024 dimensions and lower the number of results returned
Switch to Titan Embeddings G1, which uses fewer dimensions
Switch to 256 or 512 dimensions and re-embed the entire corpus

questions.scenario: Contract Q&A
questions.stem: Contract questions need precise clause matches, but the model also needs the surrounding section to interpret them. Which Knowledge Base chunking strategy fits best?
options: Fixed-size chunking with 0% overlap and a very small chunk size
Semantic chunking with the highest breakpoint threshold
Hierarchical chunking, matching small child chunks and returning their parent chunks
No chunking, so each contract is one chunk
questions.explanation: Hierarchical chunking matches on small child chunks for precision and replaces them with larger parent chunks for context. No chunking sends whole contracts and loses page-number citations.
rationales: Tiny chunks without overlap lose surrounding context.
Semantic chunking splits by meaning but does not return a larger parent context.
Correct: precise matching with broader context.
One chunk per contract hurts precision and removes page-number citations.

questions.scenario: Missing results
questions.stem: After switching a Knowledge Base to hierarchical chunking, a developer requests 10 results per query but often receives 6 or 7. What is the explanation?
options: The metadata filter is misconfigured
The vector store is throttling the Retrieve call
Several matched child chunks share the same parent, and children are replaced by their parents
Hierarchical chunking caps results at the number of source documents
questions.explanation: In hierarchical chunking, child chunks are retrieved and then replaced by their parents, so duplicates collapse and fewer results can return. This is documented behaviour, not an error.
rationales: No filter is mentioned, and the shortfall began with the chunking change.
Throttling would produce errors, not consistently fewer results.
Correct: expected behaviour of hierarchical chunking.
There is no such cap.

questions.scenario: Unstructured reports
questions.stem: A research portal ingests long reports that change topic without clear headings. Fixed-size chunks often mix two topics. The team accepts higher ingestion cost for better splits. Which option fits?
options: No chunking
Semantic chunking, which splits on meaning using a foundation model
Hierarchical chunking with a very large parent size
Default chunking with zero overlap
questions.explanation: Semantic chunking splits text where meaning changes, using buffer size and a breakpoint percentile threshold. It costs extra because it uses a foundation model, which the team accepts.
rationales: One chunk per report makes retrieval imprecise.
Correct: meaning-based splits, at extra ingestion cost.
Large parents still contain mixed topics.
Default chunking is size-based and would still mix topics.

questions.scenario: Citation gap
questions.stem: A team configured a Knowledge Base with the "no chunking" strategy. Users now complain that citations never show page numbers. Why?
options: The embeddings model does not support PDFs
Page numbers require a reranking model
With no chunking each document is one chunk, so page-number citations are not available
Citations are only available with Provisioned Throughput
questions.explanation: The no-chunking strategy treats each document as one chunk, and the documentation notes there are no page-number citations in that case. Switching to a chunking strategy restores them.
rationales: The issue is chunking, not file format.
Reranking changes order, not citation granularity.
Correct: documented consequence of no chunking.
Citations are a Knowledge Base feature, not tied to PT.

questions.scenario: Custom enrichment
questions.stem: Before indexing, every chunk must have a product code extracted from its text and added as metadata, using company-specific rules. Which approach fits Bedrock Knowledge Bases?

Use semantic chunking, which adds metadata automatically
Use a reranking model to tag chunks with product codes
Ask the model at query time to extract the product code from each chunk
questions.explanation: Knowledge Bases support a custom transformation Lambda during ingestion for custom chunking or enrichment logic. Query-time extraction is too late for filtering and adds cost per request.
rationales: Correct: ingestion-time custom logic belongs in a transformation Lambda.
Semantic chunking changes split points; it does not apply company rules.
Rerankers score relevance; they do not write metadata.
Metadata must exist at ingestion to filter on it.

questions.scenario: Multi-tenant SaaS
questions.stem: A SaaS vendor serves many customers from one Knowledge Base. A customer must never receive content from another customer's documents. What is the most reliable control?
options: Add a system prompt telling the model to use only the current tenant's documents
Increase numberOfResults so the right tenant's chunks are included
Use a reranking model to push other tenants' chunks lower
Store a tenant ID in each document's metadata and apply a tenant metadata filter on every Retrieve or RetrieveAndGenerate call
questions.explanation: A metadata filter restricts the search before results reach the model, so other tenants' chunks are never retrieved. Prompts and reranking only influence the model after the data has already been retrieved.
rationales: Prompt instructions are not an access control.
More results increase the chance of leaking other tenants' content.
Reranking changes order but still passes other tenants' content.
Correct: enforced at retrieval, not by model behaviour.

Use binary embeddings
Move the department value into the chunk text

nmslib is not supported for Knowledge Bases.
Embedding type does not affect metadata filtering.
Putting the value in text does not make it filterable.

questions.stem: Developers edit prompt strings directly in application code, and a wording change last week broke output parsing in production with no easy way back. What is the best improvement?

questions.scenario: In late 2026, a team is starting a new customer-support agent built with LangGraph. It needs serverless hosting, isolation between user sessions, and support for tasks that run for a long time in the background.

Create a new Amazon Bedrock Agent and add an action group for each tool.
Run the agent in a single AWS Lambda function invoked synchronously from Amazon API Gateway.
Deploy the agent code to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime.

questions.scenario: A company has dozens of internal REST services, each with an OpenAPI specification, plus several Lambda functions. Three different agent teams want to use these as tools through MCP.
questions.stem: What is the MOST efficient way to make these available as MCP tools?
options: Register the OpenAPI specs and Lambda functions as targets in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway.
Write and host a custom MCP server for each REST service on Amazon ECS.
Paste the OpenAPI specifications into each agent's system prompt so the model can call the URLs.
Create a Bedrock Flow per service and have each agent call InvokeFlow.

rationales: Correct: Gateway converts OpenAPI specs and Lambda functions into MCP tools with little custom code.
This works but requires building and running many servers that Gateway can generate from the existing specs.
Models cannot call URLs from a prompt; tool execution must be done by code, and this exposes internal details in prompts.
Flows are workflows, not a tool protocol, and wrapping each service in a flow adds needless layers.

questions.scenario: A refunds agent can call an issue_refund tool. Compliance requires that refunds above a set amount are never issued by the agent, even if a user crafts a prompt-injection attack.
questions.stem: Which control BEST guarantees this requirement?
options: Add a strong instruction to the system prompt telling the model never to exceed the limit.
Add a denied topic called "large refunds" to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail.
Define an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Policy rule at the Gateway that rejects issue_refund calls whose amount exceeds the limit.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on refund totals and reverse refunds that exceed the limit.

rationales: Prompt instructions are probabilistic and can be overridden by prompt injection or model error.
Denied topics filter conversation content; they do not inspect tool arguments deterministically.

questions.scenario: A travel assistant built on AgentCore should remember each user's seating and meal preferences in future conversations weeks later, without the team building its own storage layer.

AgentCore Memory with a long-term memory strategy.
Send the complete history of every past conversation in each prompt.
Store preferences in the agent's local file system inside the Runtime session.

Repoint the prod alias to version 4.
Delete version 5 so that the alias falls back automatically.
Change the application to invoke the flow's working draft.
questions.explanation: Flow versions are immutable and applications call an alias, so rollback is just repointing the alias to the earlier version. No code change or rebuild is needed.
rationales: Editing the draft does not change what the alias serves and takes longer.
Correct: repointing the alias rolls back immediately with no app change.
Aliases do not fall back automatically; deleting a version an alias uses is not a rollback method.
Production should never call the mutable draft; it loses version control.

questions.stem: What is the correct order for releasing a change to an Amazon Bedrock Flow?
options: Create an alias, edit the draft, publish a version, prepare.
Edit the working draft and have applications call it directly.
Publish a version, edit it in place, then create an alias.
Edit the working draft, prepare and test it, publish a version, point an alias at the version.
questions.explanation: You edit the working draft, prepare and test it, publish an immutable version, then point an alias at that version. Applications call the alias.
rationales: An alias needs a version to point to, and preparing comes before publishing.
Calling the draft skips versioning and makes rollback hard.
Versions are immutable and cannot be edited in place.
Correct: draft, prepare and test, version, alias.

questions.scenario: An insurer automates claims: extract fields with a model, run a fraud check, and if the amount is large, wait for an adjuster to approve, which can take several days. Every step needs retries and an auditable history.
questions.stem: Which orchestration design fits BEST?
options: An AWS Step Functions Standard workflow that calls Bedrock, uses retries and catch blocks, and waits for the approval with a task-token callback.
An AWS Step Functions Express workflow with a wait loop for the approval.
A single Lambda function that calls the model, then polls a database until the adjuster approves.
A Bedrock Flow that loops until a database flag shows approval.
questions.explanation: Step Functions Standard workflows suit long-running, auditable processes, with built-in retries and a callback pattern that pauses until a person responds. Lambda has a maximum run time and Express workflows are limited to a few minutes.
rationales: Correct: Standard workflows plus task-token callbacks handle multi-day human approval with retries and history.
Express workflows are short-lived (up to five minutes) and cannot wait days.
A Lambda function cannot run for days, and polling wastes compute.
Flows are not built for multi-day human waits and audit trails; a polling loop is an anti-pattern.

questions.scenario: Each time a document lands in Amazon S3, an EventBridge rule invokes a Lambda function that summarises it with a Bedrock model. During month-end, thousands of documents arrive within minutes and many calls fail with throttling errors.
questions.stem: What change BEST improves reliability?
options: Raise the Lambda concurrency limit so more summaries run at once.
Retry failed calls immediately in a tight loop until they succeed.
Send events to an Amazon SQS queue and have the Lambda consumer read with limited concurrency, retrying throttles with exponential backoff.
Increase max_tokens on each request so fewer calls are needed.
questions.explanation: A queue absorbs the burst and limited consumer concurrency keeps request rates under the model quota, while backoff spreads retries. More concurrency or tight retries make throttling worse.
rationales: More parallel calls push harder against the token and request quotas that are already exceeded.
Immediate retries add load and amplify throttling.
Correct: buffering plus controlled concurrency and backoff smooths load.
A higher max_tokens reserves more TPM per request and reduces concurrency.
